rows.value_as_printed: Electrical-substitution cryogenic radiometer for laser power; no acoustic resonator or transducers
rows.quote: The LOCR is one of several electrically calibrated, primary reference standards used by the Optoelectronics Division for laser power and energy measurements.
rows.document_title: Houston and Livigni (2001), Comparison of Two Cryogenic Radiometers at NIST, J. Res. NIST 106, 641-647
rows.location: Section 1 Introduction (cached research/v5/cache/d8e16b89ccfd2107.txt line 133); corroborated by NIST SP 250-62 sec. 3.2.1-3.2.2 (cached research/v5/cache/e1ac56010481a43e.txt)
rows.reasoning: The operator positively states what the LOCR is: an electrical-substitution cryogenic radiometer optimized for laser power, whose optical receiver cavity sits in high vacuum behind a Brewster window (NIST SP 250-62: 'high vacuum inside the radiometer to insulate the cold interior ... eliminates any convective heat flow'). Primary acoustic gas thermometry requires a gas-filled acoustic resonator with transducers; the described instrument is a different kind of instrument with an evacuated interior. Scope-based absence, not silence.

rows.value_as_printed: Germanium resistance thermometers read by precision ac bridge circuitry in the LOCR base
rows.quote: The temperatures at the receiver and heat sink are sensed with germanium resistance thermometers (GRTs). The GRT resistance is measured using precision alternating-current bridge circuitry, located in the LOCR's base.
rows.document_title: Livigni (2003), High-Accuracy Laser Power and Energy Meter Calibration Service, NIST Special Publication 250-62
rows.location: Sec. 3.2.3 LOCR electrical calibration, PDF page ~31 (cached research/v5/cache/e1ac56010481a43e.txt lines 1655-1657); also J. Res. NIST 106 (2001): 'LOCR uses ac bridge electronics located directly under the cryostat'
rows.reasoning: NIST's own service document for this exact apparatus states that the LOCR's receiver and heat-sink GRTs are measured with a precision ac resistance bridge, and the 2001 comparison paper confirms LOCR's temperature measurement uses ac bridge electronics under the cryostat. That is an installed resistance-thermometer measurement bridge in the documented configuration. Caveat: it is the radiometer's built-in temperature-control bridge, not a standalone metrology bridge with documented ratio accuracy; the acoustic-thermometry experiment still fails on the absent acoustic module, so this does not create a false pass.

rows.value_as_printed: No sample/resonator gas-handling system: receiver cavity operates in high vacuum
rows.quote: high vacuum inside the radiometer to insulate the cold interior from the external environment, which also eliminates any convective heat flow inside the device, but necessitates the use of a window that allows the light to enter the device.
rows.document_title: Livigni (2003), High-Accuracy Laser Power and Energy Meter Calibration Service, NIST Special Publication 250-62
rows.location: Sec. 3.2.1 Basic cryogenic radiometer operating principle, PDF page ~30 (cached research/v5/cache/e1ac56010481a43e.txt lines 1553-1555); LOCR-specific vacuum by cryopumping, carbon getter and ion pump in sec. 3.2.2
rows.reasoning: The vocabulary defines this key as the pressure interval of the sample/resonator gas-handling system. The LOCR's measurement volume is deliberately kept at high vacuum (cryopumping, carbon getter, ion pump) and light enters through a Brewster window; there is no sample gas or resonator gas-handling system whose pressure could be set over 30-120 kPa. The function does not exist on this machine, so no numeric value is given (same convention as other v6_yellow numeric absences). The LN2/LHe reservoirs 'exposed to atmospheric pressure' are cryogen baths, not a sample-gas operating range.
